review:
The game is fun, it's like a moba fight style mount and blade. A lot of aspects are more or less copied directly from M&B. If you enjoy the game play loop of M&B this is enjoyable. But it's unfinished. I bought this a year ago when it was still in EA to find that half of it was in Chinese. I refunded it, and saw recently it was on sale with DLC out. I figured I'd give it another shot, and yeah still unfinished. More is translated but there's still quite a bit that's in Chinese. There's frequent stuttering and game breaking bugs. 6 dollars still isn't bad if you're a fan of the genre but I hope this helps people make an informed decision.

Edit: Google Translate app is very useful in some situations if you do want to try this game. There is a little pen next to the mic which will allow you to draw hanzi. As long as you're kind of close, the app will give you a handful of similar hanzi in the little autocorrect bar
Also the workshop is overflowing with adult NSFW mods. I mean that's cool and all, you do you, but some regular mods would be cool too. (Mouse cursor is hard as fuck to see in big battles.)

Another added note. I've now reached end game on three different saves and it's just broken. Defeated heroes/leaders recover near instantly. The game still continues when you're in a battle, but at a ridiculous rate. By the time I run to another village and take it, my original village is gone. The leaders from every other faction, despite being at war, team up constantly to attack my one village. Pretty ridiculous since if their caravans are attacked by bandits my only option is to help out the bandits. I was set on 100% completing the game but the inconsistencies and balance issues outweigh the fun now because of how broken the end game is. I can solo entire armies but it doesn't matter, because of everything that happens simultaneously outside of the battle.

Decent game but the translations are incomplete. Only 80% of the game is in English and 20% is in Chinese... There are definitely portions of the game I can't play because I can't read it. For example, all dialogue options with captives are in Chinese. I don't understand how this is a full release with DLCs without basic priorities like having a consistent language.

Just wanted to throw my hat into the ring here. Some points *Updated 12/24/2021*  

Pros:
-Great soundtrack (Like relaxing when you are traversing the world and decent during combat)

-Animations and art style are unique

-Combat looks smooth (Once you unlock more skills and troops it shines a lot more than when you first start). You can mix and match with skills and weapons.

-Translations are decent. Better than I expected.

-The classes/characters to choose from come with their own character quests so far have been interesting.

-It's neat that the Ai characters are in motion and doing their own things.

-The trait system is clean and not too simple nor complex.

-Legacy system is cool (encourages the player to make multiple characters).

-Saves on different characters are in their own categories so it's not grouped together. Makes it easy to bounce between different character saves.

-Tavern brawls are fun once you unlock a few skills and can be tricky to where you can't just spam one button to win. I like that I have to pay a little more attention to the combat in this mode. Example I can't just spam one heavy hit move to win i have to stagger the enemy then do the heavy hitting move.

-Siege mechanic is pretty simple but map is larger then normal combat maps. You start out with at least one base and then you have to break the waves of enemies down then capture their bases. 

-So far the loot feels decent (since I have a couple heroes with me and a solid squad Before that I was having trouble doing the little dungeons). 

-The game kind of wants you to not strictly follow the story quest line and that's a good thing. After putting a little more time I noticed that as I was on my way to do story mission quests, side activities that weren't in the spot were the main mission was before, were present now. I did them (weren't too hard) I got some much needed gear which helped push me through what would have been a challenging series of encounters. I tested one of my alt characters to see if those encounters were there when I got to the same mission. They weren't but other small encounters popped up. I don't know if it has to do with the day I'm on or timing or if there is something implanted code wise that offers those extras based on your character level or gear. With that being said I noticed with main story quests from that point on there were always options of other things to do that would in turn almost always give me gear.

Cons:
-Ever since the recent patch the game freezes for about a second (maybe a little less) when parts of the map (sometimes enemies) load in. It wasn't doing this as often as it does now. It used to be once in a while. Last sessions which was about a hour it happened around 7 times. 

-Cpu % went from 3-6% (It was before the patch) to spiking to 28-47% since the most recent patch. I monitor cpu usage whenever I'm gaming. My cpu is a ryzen 9 5900x. After asking a few different friends the ones that had AMD processor told me they noticed random spikes in their cpu (never lasts more than 10 seconds). While my friends with intel processors haven't experienced that but they have experienced the random freezes for a couple seconds.

-There is a lack of direction from time to time where you will be instructed to go find something or kill someone and marker doesn't work. On top of that some of the information doesn't feel accurate (example one of the stories says someone will invade your camp in a month. I hit day 34 and get a pop up that they will come in 7 days ???)

-Sometimes the characters get stuck on rocks. Run in slo motion while it's happening (kinda funny)

-There is a general inconsistency when getting information on mobs and encounters. Sometimes you can get their level other times you can't. Some areas there are small groups of enemies that are much higher level then all the other enemies near it.
-Explanations on some of the other mechanics aren't the best (I've had to resort to guides to get some of the basics down)

-There are some monsters that are supposedly on your level but are way tougher then other monsters on your level. Example did an event where you had to fight grunts (like orcs) they were only level 3 and my units are all 10+ and they almost wiped all my units out lol. They aren't even elites or unique or bosses. Just normal enemies who pound the living crap out of you.

- About 11 hours in I finally found some of the quest bugs that other players ran into. Nothing that was game breaking. In most cases I just had to leave the area and come back and then I could finish the quest. I put this under con list because it happens every so often but work around just to leave the area and come back which is a hassle if its a quest thats not near a portal to another map.

Final Thoughts:
At the end of the day this game is an indie game that is under $15 (currently $8 on sale). It's well worth the price. I'll update the game as I play more. I enjoy it for what it is. Does it have issues? Sure. Is it fun for me I dont mind it in between other games. If you like banner lord and diablo then give this a try. If you don't like it then refund it and move on. Oh and the game starts off a bit tough. It has a somewhat steep learning curve. I highly recommend going to taverns and seeing what each hero wants as a gift and get them at least ONE gift. By the time you are level 5 you'll have 1-3 items you can give to someone as a gift. Once you get your first hero it makes the game a lot easier. I want to say the mod support is pretty outstanding with the overhauls (mind you half of them are in Chinese).

 Current score: 7/10 *Dropped the score by .5 because of the random cpu spikes.

This game has good potential, but the lack of polish is insane. Some basic things, like being able to click ESC to close windows, haven't even been implemented in many of the windows.

Here's what grinded my patience for this game:
- Characters frequently get stuck on objects, and their pathfinding is atrocious.
- Sometimes your characters become stunlocked or frozen until you die, with no way to take any action.
- The trading permits are poorly implemented and serve no purpose unless you want to stay in one town.

This game has so much potential, and the concept is good. However, considering the game was released in December 2021, it really needs a more competent studio to work on it. While releasing new content is commendable, there is still a lot of work to be done to make the game playable for a wider audience.

After 26 hours in just 2 days after the English release, all I can say is that Sands of Salzaar is a true diamond in the rough.

[u] Pros: [/u]
- Very nice artwork

- So-so BGM, not very good in my opinion, but somewhat fitting and not bad.

- Combat system is a mix between old school Chinese MMORPG and light strategy, actually scratch that, the whole game is a mix between Chinese MMORPG and Mount And Blade, I love it.

- Very nice variety in troops that you can hire, and assembling a team of companions that are actually as strong as the player feels very rewarding.

-And finally, the game has achieved what Mount and Blade 2 failed to achieve, a huge, meaningful world filled with many stories and secrets for the player to explore and solve, you can actually be a wandering vagabond with no interact with the world political matters (and not feel bored after 4 hours because the contents are just repeatable battles, quests and trading) in this game. 

[u] Cons: [/u]
- Rough start: The starting of the game is currently very rough, you got plunged into a world full of unknown without any direction or help, many the player does not have enough sense of belonging and immersion at this point to start exploring without directions, especially for the players who just want to try it out for under 2 hours, thus explain why there are so many under 2 hours Not Recommended reviews.
 
- Political Relation system: The political relations will fuck you up really hard at the start if you decide to side with some random farmers or traders to kill bandits, as helping one faction will result in negative relation with factions that are at war with them, and only minus 1 point in relation would result in you being denied access to the faction's outpost. 

- Locked skill tree: I first came into this game expecting to be able to study and rise from a normal person, to an elemental wizard, or a master swordman, or whatever feels the most fun, but the game simply locks the skill tree in the starting character choosing, quite a disappointment for me.

- Shallow character progression: I played as a wandering swordman or something, and the skill tree is just 1 path, there are branches, but mostly just a passive or upgrade of the active skill that you can either take or leave, the elemental magic that you can learn around the world is a straight skill "tree" with no branches at all. The 20 level cap just add more to that shallowness.

- Unimpressive combat system: 
+ Since the amount of skills you can learn are quite limited, combat is simply a repetition of using the same skills that you 
   have used since forever, this matter become worse in later levels, when every troops become massive bullet sponges that 
   require you to spam a lot more just to kill one. 
+ The strategy aspect in sieges are fine, but almost is in-existent normal large combat, as you cannot pause when opening 
   the strategy screen.
+ Damaged enemies running away while could be somewhat realistic, is actually more annoying than fun.

[u] Suggestion: [/u] Here are some ideas that I hope would contribute something to the game 

- A starting NPC at the recommended starting location that sells the basic necessities ( low-level gears, some food... ), warns the player a bit about the game systems, and give some pointers to the opportunities around, all under the guise of a small-time merchant that trying to sell their stuffs for newcomers to the land.
 
- An encyclopedia for the troops, monsters and systems so that the players can look deeper into the game.

- Skill trees expansion, and the ability to start as a nobody and being able to study whatever powers they want. (with, or without restriction)

- Pause when using strategy. Might not be as realistic, but since the speed of the battle is so fast, using strategies are currently very hard for new players.

- Enemies running away when damaged makes sense, but it's better to tune it down a bit, allowing the player to have more time to deal damage.

[u] Conclusion: [/u]
- While there are many features that needs more refining, the game itself is currently very enjoyable if you made it past the start (or just experiment with the first save, then starts for real in the second).

- One more good point of the game is that there are very few bugs, nothing game-breaking on my experience, though there are some lags when starting to play.

- So if you enjoy Mount and Blade gameplay but wish for a bit more RPG, and don't mind a bit of gaming hardship then this is truly the game for you. 

Tl;dr:
- Good game
- Needs more refinements
- Recommend

TLDR : Game's janky as hell, but hey, wuxia mount&blade.

+ It does what you'd expect from a mount&blade game : run errands, hire companions & troops, conquer cities and build improvements, talk with big shots and perform percussive diplomacy
+ Actual variety of combat playstyle across classes, good variety of skills and spells
+ Surprisingly good variety in NPC and companion character design, one of the strongest points imo
+ Some wiggle room for builds as most equipment is viable and comes with both fixed & random passives/actives
+ Decent replayability (NG+ shop for which you get points through achievements, different stories for each class)

- Combat is clunky as all hell, you can't hide from it :
-- Movement is only possible if you find an empty area to click, and that *will* become challenging later on
-- Untargeted attacks require you to hold shift, and some weapons (smite-type) don't work with that at all and you end up hitting yourself instead of your cursor position
-- Skill animation duration and general readability is unclear, some skills vfx feel hastily put together and offer poor if not no impact feedback
-- Rolling out of telegraphs to dodge attacks works when RNJesus says it does. Spinning in circles very close to the boss / enemy pack has proven more effective than any attempt at arena-game style combat.
-- Getting CC-locked (stunlocked, frozen on repeat or juggled) is a thing and will mess you up. Thankfully you have items to reduce CC duration below 0% and passives to render you immune to freeze and the like. You'll get frozen anyway.
-- Squad orders limited to "attack/defend/follow", no tactical positioning options, you have to drag the actual squad behind you with "follow" and sit them down with a "defend" order. Not that it matters as both armies clash within the first 10 seconds of every fight anyway. Enemy only knows "charge".

- Exploration is a bit limited (there will be 30 landmarks per map which are just repeat copies of some 4-5 biome-appropriate landmarks) and environments are cliché (Plains, Swamp, Tundra, Desert)
- Bad pathfinding unless you're traveling from city to city
- Story missions, dialogue, cutscenes, scene transitions, etc feel *very* amateurish and will leave you wanting for better moodsetting. Actual plot is good though.
- The main modding scene is chinese, and unless you're able to read it you'll be limited to the crumbs translators had the patience to port to english (often outdated and unmaintained)

All in all, it's a game with great ambition and a very solid amount of enjoyable content, but it brutally lacks polish and is less enjoyable for the english audience. Would still recommend if you can deal with and look past all the clunk.

Yes, it's a Chinese game similar to Mount&Blade.
Yes, the world map is smaller.
Yes, the characters only have 3 equipment slots (Accesory, Armor, Weapon).
Yes, there are also fewer ways to interact with the world.
Yes, the combat is like in mobile games.
Surprising, right? You've found a game, development cost of which was times less than Mount&Blades's. 
So why would you even consider playing it? Well, first of all, Sands of Salzaar doesn't try to be a Mount&Blade alternative. 
It's a pure sandbox with its own general storyline, which you can ignore and just wander around the world. Choose a class(some of which have unique personal storylines) or play as Nameless to create a monster that solos everyone and everything. Complete quests, progress through the skill/talent trees, capture cities, manage them. Repeat with another character on higher difficulty.
Yes, there are some bugs.
Yes, sometimes the game balance seems unfair.
And Yes, you should try out this game.

This game could've been a good homage to Mount and Blade. Unfortunately, this game suffers from one specific problem so much it outweighs all upsides it has. In fact, it is so bad I decided to spend some time putting a thumb down. 
The issue that completely and utterly destroys the game for me is tracking down characters. At its best, it's frustrating. At its worst, it's infuriating. 
The game works similar to M&B, so much of the gameplay revolves around interacting with the lords. You might remember how much pain in the ass it is to track down a certain lord in that game. Well, they managed to make it even worse in this game. Imagine or not, it's possible. Yes, just like M&B, you can ask around about the whereabouts of a mofo you need to talk to, but 9 out of 10 times you will just receive nothing better than: "he is somewhere in region X". Yes, that's right. It is as if you were told: "The character you are looking for is somewhere in Aserai Desert", so feel free to go comb the whole thing (spoiler alert: they left Aserai Desert two hours ago). If you are extremely lucky, they will be in one of the cities, which makes the process bearable.
What triggered me to finally write this review, though, and also abort a ten-hour long campaign is the next ingenious feature: you can't ask about the location of someone you haven't met personally. So if you need to talk to someone, but you haven't met them, you can only hope to stumble upon them randomly. Do you realize how absurd it is? It is as you were playing M&B, but could not ask about the location of a faction leader because you have never happened to cross ways with them. And they can literally be anywhere. Right now I am at the point where the main quest wants me to go talk to a guy, who is a faction leader, by the way, and who I've never met in 150 game days. I am literally brought to a stall because I realize that looking for him blindly might as well take dozens of real-time hours. Sorry, I can't afford such a sacrifice.

The game is definitely rough around the edges, and has some glaring issues: stuff like the pathfinding sucking at times. The auto walk usually works fine, but I have on quite a few occasions had other armies following me, only to get stuck on a nearby tree, and I had to run around and order them back and force trying to get them unstuck. This occurs both in the open world and in the combat. It works 90% of the time, but you'll definitely notice it when it fails.
There is also some QOL I  REALLY with the game would add, such as being able to change the equipment of your other leaders in your faction when you have your own faction. You can recruit them into your team, and change their gear that way, but needing to pull them into your team, change the gear, then go to the menu, find out what town they were from, and do the dialogs to send them back, is quite a bit of effort - especially when you have 30-40 people to do it for... [h1]Pathfinding[/h1]

Unit pathfinding remains one of the game's greatest achievements.

The logic is foolproof:

[b]A → B.[/b]

If an obstacle happens to be between A and B, continue walking towards B.

With sufficient determination — and presumably enough lubricant applied to the units — they may eventually slide around the obstacle to the left or right. This process can take anything between a moment and the heat death of the universe.

What makes this considerably funnier is that the developers then designed battle maps seemingly intended to [i]maximize exposure to their own pathfinding problem[/i].

You get C-shaped layouts full of fences, towers and corners that units cannot properly navigate around, or enormous rock formations placed directly in front of the army's spawn point.

The battle starts and your formation immediately partitions itself into three civilizations:

The left side walks left.
The right side walks right.
The middle group embraces the rock.

Everyone eventually hopes to meet again on the other side.

This isn't some rare edge case where the AI encounters an unfortunate piece of terrain. Obstacles are deliberately placed exactly where large groups of units need to move.

Bad pathfinding in a game with huge armies is understandable. Building giant rocks, fences and C-shaped obstacle courses directly into the routes those huge armies are expected to take is where it becomes performance art.

[h1]Progression and farming[/h1]

The problem is not that the game allows you to build absurdly powerful characters.

The problem is that it asks for an absurd amount of farming to reach those builds while giving you almost nothing that actually requires them.

You can farm rare equipment, permanent attributes, enchantments, squad jewels, jewel slots, the correct slot colors, refine jewels through multiple tiers and optimize increasingly specific unit combinations.

Some equipment requirements are ridiculous. Wildsand Armor, for example, requires 250 Strength. A heavily developed character can have excellent Strength equipment and permanent stat bonuses and still be nowhere near wearing it.

Jewels are another level of farming entirely. There are lots of different jewels in the game, but in practice [b]all[/b] farming sources are determined to hand you the same few jewels over and over again. You can farm dozens upon dozens of drops while the specific jewel you actually want might as well be a mythical creature.

Then, once you finally have the jewel, perhaps you need several copies to equip all squads. And perhaps you first need the correct inset slot. And perhaps you need another rare item to add that slot.

All of this would be perfectly fine if there were some corresponding endgame difficulty waiting for you.

There isn't.

By the time you have farmed enough permanent stats to equip the absurd equipment, obtained and refined the rare jewels, fixed your squad slots and assembled the army these progression systems appear to be designed around, you could have conquered the entire world already.

Several times.

Late-game bosses aren't really the obstacle either. A reasonably developed army already destroys them long before you've finished optimizing anything.

So the progression curve ends up backwards:

[b]"I need to farm for another 20 hours so that I can become powerful enough to efficiently defeat things I was already effortlessly defeating 20 hours ago."[/b]

The farming therefore isn't really progression towards overcoming the game. It becomes a separate collection/min-maxing exercise you do because you want to finish a build.

The game gives you an enormous optimization treadmill and then forgets to put anything at the end of it that requires the optimized character.

[h1]The frustrating part[/h1]

There is actually a lot here that I like. The troop system, character building, faction warfare and all the strange combinations of skills, equipment and units can be genuinely interesting.

That's exactly why the state of the game is so frustrating.

The underlying systems invite you to experiment with them, but then you run into broken descriptions, inconsistent translations, questionable mechanics, extreme RNG, unfinished systems and bugs that have survived for years.

Instead of polishing the enormous amount of content that already exists, development repeatedly seems to move sideways into another feature or DLC.

There is a genuinely interesting game buried in here.

Unfortunately, after hundreds of hours, I increasingly feel that I've spent as much time studying which parts of it actually work as I have playing it.

The genre is also hard to describe - the best idea I have is a mix of rimworld and sacred, but extremely simplified. To be short, there are different tribes in the game and you can see the activity on the map. These tribes will wage war against each other, trade and interact in many different ways. You can, if you want, join one of them, or found your own. If you choose to found your own tribe, you'll be put into a tough situation that's very hard to combat as every clan will basically be at war with you, but once you've survived this and expanded a bit, it's very rewarding to see your own units run around the map and interact with the other tribes.

The combat system is a bit janky, to be fair - CC is not clearly shown to you and sometimes you'll wonder: "Why the hell can't I move?". CC chains are also not very uncommon (shoutout to dhib frost archers I hate you all), which can be quite frustrating. However, once you got a hang of it, it's quite fun to play, even tho fights in the later game are very easy.

There is a total of 7 different characters you can play with from teh start, each with their own skill tree and starting benefits/disadvantages and the option to learn other skill trees from teachers in the open world. The bounty hunter, for example, has a very strong early game with his skills, but has negative standing with all tribes, making them attack you on sight. This gives each new playthrough another dynamic and changes how you play the game and in which region you start. Also, there is another character you can unlock after you finish the game once. Also, it's possible to unlock legacy points, and you can use those legacy points to "power up" your future playthroughs with better gear, more starting resources or strong heroes already in your squad.

Story is okay from what I can tell, however, nothing mindblowing. Can't say anything else about it.

Now, not everything is great about the game. The UI, for example, is horrendous. In order to control your tribe and members, you have to go through a bunch of textboxes. While this does work, it's really not state of the art an I can imagine that there is a much better way to do that. Also, the dialogue between your heroes (strong NPCs you can have in your squad) is basically always there same. There is a variety of 4 - 5 different dialogues (at least with my heroes, apparently different heroes have different "personalities" and the dialogue may change with other heroes) and in the end, you just pick the option that will make the person that likes you the most happier so they stay with you. There is not really anything to it and it's just a rather boring side product.

However, considering that the game only costs 12.50€, I can't fault the devs for these problems, especially because many of them (like the messed up translations) are easiely fixable. Overall, the game we have here is amazing and it's something you can dump a lot of hours into, if you like the genre.

I've bought this game many years ago, while exploring chinese single player games. Since EA I still enjoy it and replay it once in a while, despite its shortcomings.

Speaking of which, most of the problems are related to the english translation, including borked quest(lines). Generally such problems can be fixed by temporally switching to chinese or following guides. Main culprit here is Spirit Witch's questline. So don't start your first playthru of the game on 'expert mode' (1 save file). It is not as bad as it may sound after reading this, but still it is better to be warned.

SoS is essentially a sandbox, where you start as a small guy in a land that is in a constant state of war between several factions. Comparisons to Mount and Blade series are not too farfetched here. You slowly build your character and the size and quality of your army along the way to the top, while doing unique and/or repeatable quests, exploring points of interest and all that jazz.

What I find really interesting is the troop upgrade system which is similar to some old game called Disciples. Once your squad of farmers got enough exp, you can upgrade it by choosing a certain path on a troop upgrade tree, range, cavalry, support or melee branch to make it simple. Of course, the class of your character can affect your troops, for instance Spirit Witch can make ALL arcane-type or summon-type units to apply Terror on attacks. But thats not all. Besides the fact that you can equip ur character, you can also.. slot gems in your troops, sometimes drastically changing their features. Like a gem, which shields your troop once they below 50%, or the one which make them shock opponents with their skills and attacks. Keep in mind that some troops have a very simple upgrade path, like dragons for example, but they are dragons so, yeah.

Combat is similar to top down arpgs and MOBAs, depending on the encounter, you either fight alone (with hired heroes) or with all your troops. Of course, with experience you can easily destroy half of the enemy army yourself. Several quickcast options can be found in options, and you will need em, cause you will use your skills A LOT.

Another clever thing here is the LEGACY system. Basically, you have a set of achievements you can complete on your run, no matter what mode you are playing (story, with a questline or a sandbox). Every successfull achievement will reward you with LP (legacy points), which can be spent before starting a new playthru. This way you can start with more resources, skillpoints, better reputation with factions, buy unique skills or even skill trees.

The game as you can understand now have a lot of interesting and interconnected features which can be talked about forever, but lets talk about DLC's for a bit. What I personally recommend as a base is a free Champions of Chaos DLC which simply makes the game better when it comes to your character or the one you hire. You can also learn the ENTIRE skilltree from the unique heroes even if u don't hire them, as long as you have a good relationship with em. Another DLC, which is kind of 'safe' to recommend is Ember saga, specifically Ember Workshop part of it. Tournament and Eclipse are both fine, the latter though suffers from small translations issues still and kinda grindy and not in a very fun way.

So once in a game menu, make sure to turn on Champions of Chaos, Ember Workshop.  Everything else is once you've tasted the game enough. Of course, DLCs can be turned on and off, but don't do that during the playthru.

As deep as the game may seem after reading all above, the world itself is sadly as deep as a puddle, not much UNIQUE stuff to explore, so mostly it is better to lean your gameplay to combat scenarious or following the main/class questline (if it has one). But that can be said about any sandbox, just find your own fun.

To be fair, I didn't plan to write a review on Sands of Salzaar, but after all these years, seeing recent reviews as 'mixed' is simply made me sad. Yes, I wish bugs were fixed and all, but even with them, for this price, it is an extremely good deal.

I love Mount and Blade. I don't love, but definitely enjoy plenty, ARPGs.

The problem is that this game just isn't remotely good at either. Well, it's maybe a *passable* sandbox for 5-10 hours, before your character outgrows it and it just starts to feel like a waste of time. But as an ARPG if someone told me this was an alpha they made in a month, I'd tell them the controls still feel way too stilted, and they should try to make fewer, more in-depth classes so you can actually get some feeling of real choices and gameplay. Movement is so clunky you'll mostly stick to just pressing your 2-5 buttons at the biggest clump of enemies for 30 hours of gameplay.

Combat is short, messy, and usually either obnoxiously hard or agonizingly easy. The introduction of a lot of raw level numbers into an open sandbox takes the "this basic monster is randomly 20 levels too high" problem up to 11. I can't even force myself to finish the main story because it's just be fast-forwarding back and forth across the world doing 15 second at a time zero-effort battles where I need two buttons.

I tried a number of different characters and mostly they either sucked, or went wildly out of control right away. And I imagine the ones that seemed bad just take an extra hour to go wildly over the top. The max difficulty does nothing to help.

Basic combat just isn't fun. It's a very clunky and stilted ARPG with an absolutely tiny variety of options in the moment. The army-building side has potential, but really "just get as many heroes as you can and throw them at the enemy" will beat almost everything you run into. Keeping up with gear durability is a drag, food spends 90% of the time being irrelevant and 10% of the time being annoying, partial squads and combining is just obnoxious.

And all the mods are in Chinese so unlike some other games there's no chance in hell of me finding a fan rebalance mod that makes there actually be a video game with compelling combat.

Basically, imagine an ARPG you enjoyed. Remember what it was like to fight mobs at level 5? You probably had a couple of abilities with simple interactions, but it probably wouldn't be fun if you had to keep going with no interesting gear drops or anything new, and also wonky pathfinding, right? That's all of the combat in this game forever.

The open world sandbox will challenge you for a moment, but once you accrue a bit of power the challenge is gone. Most quests are very simple "go talk to person" or "go clear out location" or maybe the weirdly common "bring me X of X flower" (fortunately I already obsessively stockpile flowers).

Those hours I have on this game are partially spent AFK or such, but in large part spent restarting as different characters on max difficulty hoping to just find myself having an interesting challenge. In the game, turning up difficulty beyond just picking the hardest initial option apparently requires you to beat the game repeatedly before you can go further, which I have no interest in doing. Imagine a 15+ hour action game that forced everyone to beat "Very Easy" and then "Easy" and then "Normal" before it would let them actually experience a moment of resistance, not to mention knowing the game inside out by the time it would've had a chance to challenge them and likely cheesing it to death.

There's real moments of brightness in there - getting your first couple of heroes and trying to customize them a bit to click together, going after your first bandit camp or two and trying to decide how much to put your soldiers to use (although the actual only threat in any camp is just wildly high HP and high damage towers that you'll spend half the battle mindlessly bashing as it kills people)...

Everywhere I look the game is overflowing with charm and potential, and every attempt to look deeper sees a clunky mess that I don't think I should have any reason to expect further development to rectify. I still like the idea of the game. I'd *love* to pit my army against worthy adversaries, using my own character's skills to try to turn the tide. I'd love to roam the world, finding locations, making allies, accruing power, etc - if only I didn't reach max level in a blink and just be stuck in a world where the only chance at resistance would just be bashing my head against a hyper-fortified faction capital or something (faction leaders are chumps who could kill maybe like two individual soldiers before I mass magic aoe their entire army to death).

Argh. It's hard to even stop writing a review like this, because every part of the game I think of reminds me of one thing I really like and three things that frustrated me.

At the time of this review, it is an Early Access Game. I am reviewing it much earlier than my normal time frame (which is around 100 hours), but I feel in this case, that is fine.

This game, if you need to compare it, is like a story heavy top down version of Mount and Blade. There are huge amounts of similarities to Mount and Blade when it comes to game play mechanics. Obviously the art style is its own, which appears to me mostly, if not a totally hand drawn type of art, although its not pencil and paper type of hand drawn, this seems to be of pretty good quality.

The music honestly gets a little redundant, it has the same background music for multiple territories rather than a new music for every territory, although this is fixed by mods. But the music in and of its self is pretty decent.

The combat feels like what a top down Mount and Blade would feel like, only you play your character more like you would in a Diablo game. Combat wise, you would have to imagine mixing Diablo with Mount and Blade. Since its an early access game occasionally you run into little issues like suddenly losing your ability to move for a bit (not to be confused with purposeful loss caused by crown control skills), although I suspect this will be patched out in the very near future.

The game has some other mechanics in it, such as romance, although its highly undeveloped at this time. Basically, you give a chick tons of gifts, then you confess to her and you two become boyfriend/girlfriend......and.....that's kind of it, aside from like 2 lines of text that are different, there's nothing else to be done. I suspect this is a feature they will develop more over time, and I also put some suggestions in their discord, so I believe that this will be addressed in the future.

Performance wise, its a pretty low demand game, so you wont really run into any lag, I never ran into any lag and if you look at the spec's required for this game, you can tell that you don't really need much to run this game.

The story line is longer than you would think it is, and there are multiple stories that you can delve into it that would be considered main (There's a  main quest and then there's character quests). Of course, like every other game in existence, you have a plethora of side quests you can do. Although, if you were to compare to a game like Mount and Blade, the story in this is far more developed. You could technically play this simply for the story and not the sandbox if you really wanted.

As for mods, like many other game, especially sandbox ones, mods are a huge boon to the game. The same stands true for this game as well. Since this game is Chinese primary, their English translation may be a little off, which is where mods come into play. Some mods are entirely devoted to upgrading the quality of English translations so they make sense to the English players. There are also mods of every other sort of type like one would expect in a sandbox type game, such as character re-draws, item spawners, level cap increases, map additions etc etc, although most of them are written in Chinese so you have to look int eh comments to see what they do half the time. One of the benefits this game has though is that it has a Mod section in the main menu for you to develop the mods using the actual game its self and not a third party program (although they tell you what you need in the same in-game menu of you want to use third party programs for more advanced mods), so if you wanted to make a custom mod, it should not be too difficult for you to do yourself if you cant find it (or upload to steam even).

Without giving out too many details about the game, I will leave the above as it is. However, even in its early access state, I would suggest this game is playable and can be enjoyed as it totes a completed story line (although I did make suggestions to add to it for personal preference). But if you are on the fence, and you like games like Diablo or Mount and blade (or both), then you will most likely like this game as well, so long as you are able to accept the art style of this game. Just keep in mind though, this is still early access and new features and improvements will be coming (I still see updates fairly frequently).

This is a great game, and if the devs keep building on it, it will become incredible, but it gives you virtually no help/guidance, so I've decided to share some of the key things I've learned since starting the game last week. Hopefully these tips can prove useful to new players:

1) The start is going to be ROUGH. You're going to want to explore and get drawn off into the vast world on offer, but you'll find yourself out of your depth and failing quests pretty quickly if you're not careful. Stick with your main character quests and the Redstone keep area whilst you level up, otherwise you'll end up with a dead squad and lost reputation with factions. Don't worry, once you level up, you'll feel more powerful and it's a pretty decent power curve depending on your character class.
2) Don't be afraid to take on basic units for 150Utar - they will grow with you and can be levelled up into very powerful units. 
3) Keep hold of anything you receive as a 'gift' when raiding/questing - they are usually items of interest that you can give to potential party members to win them over. One example is the combat gloves/helmet etc. - you can gift those to a female character in the Eastern Umbra Cliffs with red hair (I forget her name) and she will join you.
4) Don't go seeking out any quest and hoarding quests as many have timers (it will tell you, but only AFTER you accept the quest) - many will be beyond your capabilities for a while, so better to come back later once you're Lvl 15+
5) In Umbra Cliffs you can find Ultimate Forge Hammers easily which will repair any equipment, so if you find yourself with a decent piece of gear with low durability, head down there and stock up.
6) Utar is tight at first, a great way to get more is to ask town Chiefs for quests and sometimes they will give you a quest about a kidnapped noble with a 1,000 Utar reward. They will give you 1,000 Utar (which you can spend if you want and go rogue) which if you then deliver to the Bandits who kidnapped the noble, will net you a 1,000 Utar reward with no fights and minimal work. Easy 1,000 Utar, plus reputation gain. 
7) Another easy early quest to look out for are ones about groups of teenagers that have run away, they will usually be easy to find (one set to the right of town, left of town and below the town). You get an easy fight for XP, then nice XP, Utar and reputation gain upon completion which is pretty quick.
8) Trading is the best way to boost your Utar - from Redstone buying the pepper is an affordable investment, then head north and you can sell it for a significant profit at the Golden Bazaar or another town near the top of the map. Similarly, taking something from the far South towns up North is easy money too.
9) You can fast travel. Press M to open the map, then right click on a location and select 'Move Here' then press 'T' and it will massively fast forward time so you get there v fast.
10) If you have a dead unit, you can revive them with a White Rose potion - I'd recommend getting early talents in the healing tree which will give you 2 potions every week, so that you can revive units if you find yourself regularly getting into tough fights.
11) Look out for Bandits attacking trade caravans - you can join the fight to assist the caravan for nice XP and loot - they are usually quite easy fights as you get help from the trader's party.
12) Once you're lvl 5+ attacking the Prisons to free captives is a good way to get free new units for your army.
13) If you come across a villager wanting wood in the Umbra Cliffs, don't give them any until you have a HUGE amount as I have almost 1,000 wood with no result.
14) To capture a camp you will see several control points once you attack it - simply go and hold each one until it turns green (Domination style) - if your units aren't doing what they want or you want them to push to take a point, select 'All Units' then 'Attack' to get them moving as sometimes they will just stand there.
15) Don't worry too much about Talent Point allocation as you get a seemingly endless supply regardless of level cap. They are all strong trees and there's no 'best starting tree' as it depends what you'll be focusing on first (trade vs more characters in party vs large army etc.)

There's still a way to go and the combat could certainly be improved with units running endlessly into walls etc. but it's well worth your time and money - plenty of replayability and quest galore. I haven't tried taking over a town for myself yet but will be giving that a go soon too. Enjoy!

Well-thought-out and well-written, but not very well-executed. Every time I come across an idea in this game that would easily put Mount and Blade to shame, I find some annoying flaw that ruins it.
For example, characters get stuck in geometric details on the global map and tactical map. 
During a tavern brawl, the southern wall of the building obscures your character and your opponent, forcing you to guess what they are doing. 
Once the plot becomes interesting, they begin to deliver it through text.
In places, the translation is surprisingly good, in other places, the text is not translated at all. 
You can minimize the game to tray, but no one guarantees that you will be able to maximize the window back. 
While exploring a cave, you may be ambushed by the "creatures that dwell in the dark". The dark creatures turn out to be city guards. 
There is no autoattack. Click the enemy to death (and your mouse too). 
And so on.

Speaking of Mount and Blade, it consists of two main parts: an adventure simulator on a global map and tactical battles. Salzaar is mostly the first and it's done well (except from getting stuck). Tactical battles here are not very tactical, they are chaotic brawls full of ability abuse. 

So here is Salzaar. Sometimes genius, sometimes shameful. It's grindy. It is definitely playable, but also very facepalmable. For me technical execution of a game is very important, so I can't recomend it. Otherwise, I would.

As someone who has a hundred hours on this game, I have say, right now I do not recommend this game. For several reasons, the first of which is it's combat. Combat gets very boring towards the end of the game as it starts feeling less like gameplay and more of a stat check, both for the individual battles and the army battles. 

The second reason is that the writing is really bad. Like, really, really bad. Most characters have absolutely zero depth, and the quests are all either shallow or vague, melodramatic, convoluted nonsense that often becomes completely incoherent. 

Finally, let me go into the setting and look of the game. The game looks bad. Some of the zone, Umbra Cliffs especially look horrendous. And it's not just the setting, I don't mind gloomy looking swamp levels in other games and wouldn't rate the game's art down simply because a setting is gloomy looking. I mean level and art design decisions are bad. For example the main river looks horrendously out of place. Don't get me wrong the river is a bad looking in the other areas but looks even worse in Umbra Cliffs because it's blue screen color looks so out of place and got me looking at the other part the map which looks like the person who made it just took one dark green color and splotched a bunch of lighter green colors on top of it without caring about what the final product would look like. There's no logic in where they colored using their color pallet. For example, in one area, there's a bunch of light green splotches which is suppose indicate that this area is wetter, but by the river itself which is suppose to be the wettest place it goes from the darkest green color straight into the computer screen blue colored river which they should have darkened for Umbra Cliffs but didn't.

Finally, there was the setting which I initially excited and was hoping to learn more about the factions. But I eventually found out, that all of the faction lore is completely superficially and suffers from the problems with the plot in that it is always told but not shown. For example Jamal City which the plot and other character repeatedly mentioned is never visited once during the game despite it supposedly being the seat of the Nasir faction and capital of Salzaar: the name of the whole region. None of the factions leaders, in any quest or dialogue take any action regarding it, despite it supposedly being a very important city. 

Furthermore, all the all regions the feel the same once you get past the intial tile swap. You don't a feeling of cold when you visit the Zargos Mountains, it doesn't feel hot in the North East Desert that I forgot the name of. And I'm not complaining that there isn't a climate system, I'm complaining because it doesn't feel like the people there have a different lifestyle or culture from the people living elsewhere. And there are a ton of design decisions they could have taken to do that. For example having the people residing in those areas wear different clothes since one is snowy and the other is supposedly a really hot desert. Instead they all wear the same clothes, and what's worse none of the people seem to care about the other regions or even mention that there's a major civil war going on after the main government who previously ruled all of Salzaar collapsed. 

The main quest hammers you over the head with vague platitudes about the "horrors of war" but none of the people in Salzaar seem to care about it in the slightest. In fact, outside of the main quest, I don't think a single other character even mentions there is a war going on. Caravans coming from one faction are fully willing to travel and trade with cities of factions they are at war with. I've been told to deliver supplies from one settlement to a settlement of a faction they at war with the same gravity of being told to milk a cow. And when I became the head of my own factions, I could wander around freely in a region entirely controlled by my enemies, without a care in the world. I could even sneak into their towns, talk with the enemy lords and mayors and do requests for them as if nothing was going on between us. Which is why I say that the characters, setting, and plot are extremely superficial and bad. The very textbook example of tell but don't show. 

There are other examples I can give of bad writing, but I think you get the gist already. Overall, I do not recommend this game.

Lots of potential (whoever thought of Diablo crossed with Mount & Blade is a genius) here, but it needs quite a bit more polish. 

There is a general air of sloppiness to the design of this game. Here are a few examples that I ran into in my 3-4 hours of play.

-Pathfinding is problematic, with units occasionally getting stuck inside of walls (funny in the overworld, but potentially fatal in battles), and in one instance, the pathfinding actually gave up when I tried to path through a very narrow canyon.

-Mouse controls have issues. Left and right buttons do the same thing (instead of having one do movement, and one do interactions). This is an issue when most of the battlefield is covered in enemies, and instead of avoiding the angry sword man who is determined to separate your head from your shoulders, your character instead auto-attacks a nearby mob. Additionally, when hovering over buildings and towns in the overworld, the game will pop up a helpful tooltip. However, the tooltip blocks mouse clicks, and is anchored to the structure, instead of the mouse (and the camera keeps the party in the middle of the screen at all times), so if you approach a town from the west and try to click on it, the tooltip will shout, "Get down Mr. President!", jump in front of the mouse cursor, and block your click. Very annoying.

-Some attack animations are very restrictive, locking the character in place for too long, and generally just interrupting the flow of battle. This issue was far more noticeable with the Inn "Brawl" skills, in my experience.

-Translation needs to be finished/edited. I encountered a fair number of UI elements that either weren't translated at all, had obvious spelling errors, didn't have formatting, or used very odd word choices. The biggest offender was the Talent window (which you'll be frequenting a lot throughout the game). The "accept" and "cancel" buttons are not translated. Now, this isn't really a huge obstacle (you'll figure out which is which pretty quick), but it points the sloppiness of the design. It's incredible how this was missed, considering how often and how quickly players will run into it.

-Minor performance issues. I encountered semi-frequent micro-stutters (especially while fast forwarding). Also, for some reason, scrolling out while fully zoomed out causes stutters. Also, I ran into what felt like a memory-leak of some sort (performance steadily degraded after a couple hours of continuous play).

All of these issues combine to make for an experience that is half playing a fun game, and half wrestling with the controls and the UI. This is a real shame, because the game, when I actually got to play it, was quite fun and engaging. It felt like there was a lot of content, with hidden treasures and encounters scattered around the map (and often unmarked, so there's meaningful exploration, instead of just following waypoints).

TL;DR: Needs a few gallons of polish, but there's a great game in here.

A Wild, Wacky Desert Romp
Sands of Salzaar on Steam is a chaotic, gorgeous open-world RPG that hooked me from the start. 
I dove in blind, ignoring guides, and spent hours fumbling through its vibrant desert world, leading my ragtag army of wolves and mages into battles that felt like Dynasty Warriors on a 2D acid trip. 
The art is stunning, the freedom to conquer or befriend factions is thrilling, and the janky translation only adds to its quirky charm. 
I lost countless hours exploring, laughing when I accidentally pissed off a tribe, then won them over with a shiny rock. It’s not perfect—bugs and vague quests can frustrate—but the joy of discovering this sandbox gem solo makes every misstep worth it. 
If you love getting lost in a game, give this a spin. You’ll thank me later.

The game is less sand boxy and more of an arms race. You either focus on completing the story efficiently or taking the game slow and steady as you work up to mass supremacy. The arms race aspect is largely on getting the squad of heroes you want for the team you want before they get locked into other factions and break neck sprinting to areas of interest (cough, dragons). Sometimes you can pull the locked heroes out of those factions, other times you can't (maybe). Also, there are quite a few bugs, usually small ones if you save you're game every 3-6 in game days. Try not to get tripped up my any translation errors, there's a few. It's an exceptional game for a pretty decent price that does a lot of random things. Some of those random things are fun, like the scorpion rock (not the location) in the desert area. Other things less fun, like the total lack of balancing or accurate representation of threat level for side events or quests. Nothing like that level 5 dryad encounter reminding you that level 5 could be considerably worse than say a level 20 giant encounter. The learning curve in this game can be steep, other times its obvious. Jade for example is a barrier for fun troops, and knowing how to get fun troops is another barrier. To get jade to upgrade troops you can disband certain monster groups in towns for considerable jade bonus (portal in snowy area troops for best results), you can re-loot previous on map jade pick ups after a few days, you can recruit the Amira Zahra (starting companion choice ,very expensive kinda worth it) and upgrade her jade talents 1 upgrade on the left side of the tree 3 on the right side for a weekly bonus of 35 jade (maybe more). Amira can teach you her talent tree which I have not done for her yet, but I assume this also includes at least one of her jade talents for the plus 5 a week. As for how you get cool or fun soldiers, the level barrier for the nasty monster dungeons is rough, but some special events in the swamp based on current weather do drop monsters (as a cost, keep a white rose potion handy), and you can hire tree people in Amaranth town in Dakn territory in the far North. I have also see other unique soldiers sold by random mercenary captains far less frequently elsewhere. There are special beast trainers in the Northern territories that refresh weekly. Fun fact, you can befriend the bandits in this game by bullying them then letting them go at which point you then recruit them for decent troops. Other heroes besides merchant lady who are mind bogglingly useful, Mousa for charge talent on all heavy troops, that creepy ten year old girl who never blinks who gives you a skill point every week(?), other people who give monster, beast, or broad soldier or armor buffs (cough Batu). If your struggling to learn how to play the game, try the berserker class its a single really good button. If this seems boring, remember you can learn other button later if you so desire. Its a fun game that feels like a mix of Avatar aesthetic with Mountain & Blade Warband and Diablo mechanics. Its fun not perfect.

The unfortunate thing here is that Sands of Salzaar is a good game, but I can't recommend it in it's current state.

To put it simply, I love this game. However, this game is not for everyone and certainly has some issues that may be too difficult for some players to overlook. This game is not originally in English. The translation is fine but nowhere near what you'd expect from a AAA title; some lines read poorly and quest locations can become difficult to find without a guide. Also some mechanics are poorly explained due to translation issues as well resulting in many mistakes in your first play-through. Nonetheless this game has an amazingly fun loop. Rally troops, earn favor, gain territory, and fight war; it gives you a great Mount & Blade experience that I personally enjoy more than Mount & Blade. The game has a lot of troop variety and some choices when it comes to base design. Want to be an independent Knight Errant who is wanted by all factions, you can do that; want to be a Dakn loyalist eventually being made general under Queen Rebiya, you can; want to say screw it and take a foothold in the Ifrit lands and declare war on everyone as the new big bad, you can. This game gives you the freedom to play how you want and rarely limits your decisions no matter the consequences. One game I played had ten factions running around the map and none of them were the original starting factions. The main story is serviceable but the game truly shines in Sandbox mode where you're free to play how you want; be a trader, a merc, a soldier, etc. All in all, I love this game and if you want another Mount & Blade with an Arabian Nights feel, then give this game a shot. The price is very fair for this title and I was even able to pick it up on sale.

I can say with absolute conviction that I enjoyed the game (you don't tend to spend 200 hours in a game you hate). That said, I cannot say with any degree of certainty that anyone else would enjoy the game. The game feels like it needed another 6 months in the oven before being called done and so the game has a lot of weird issues and bugginess. That said, if you are fine with dealing with the weird issues, I definitely think the game is worth getting.

The issues I am referring to are:
[list]
[*] The game is often poorly translated, incorrectly translated or not translated at all. You can still understand the overall story just fine, but you will see a lot of weirdness around the translations
[*] The game's DLC's are very buggy. For example, the Tournament DLC by my experience has about a 30% chance of not bugging out and giving out the reward for winning a tournament, which for a paid DLC? Yeah, that's pretty bad.
[*] Several of the game's features are poorly explained requiring you to looking into the game's files to understand what certain abilities or stats do (this is just poor user experience)
[*] The game has some very questionable collision at times, you can get stuck on all sorts of things or can get hit by attacks that really don't feel they should
[*] The game has boss fights and I think the devs thought that these fights would be a test of mechanical skill, but the game's controls are nowhere near tight and responsive enough for what is being asked
[*] There are also several rather unbalanced units that can do fun things like stun lock you infinitely or hit you with an effect that makes you run away for something like 20 seconds which just kills the flow of a battle
[*] The dev company is Chinese which isn't bad, but what is bad is the difficulty in communicating with them that comes from the language barrier and the weird product laws that come out of China. Best example for this is that the game has name censorship. A single player game, censors you. Yep. (T_T)
[/list]

And despite all of these issues, I still enjoyed the game. Not a whole lot of games that can have so many issues and still be fun if you ask me.

A lot of the items that are in the dungeons just flat out do not drop. They are listed as possible loot but, even after google searching, they just.. don't.

There are many that fall into this category. If you fail it, there are no do-overs. In fact, one of the very first quests you  get puts you in negative standing with one of two factions based on who's side you choose. On this note, the color of the cursor- it matches the color of the sand in the desert. I would like to start by saying that I hate this game. I did not find the game play fun. It's kind of like Mount and Blade but Mount and blade is far more tactical and the combat in this game is akin to watching a toddler smashing two cars together. Whoever has the bigger stronger army is going to win. That being said I can see how someone might find the game play to be mindless fun and might not want a complicated tactical rpg. The real problem with Sands of Salzaar is the story. The story for Sands of Salzaar is bad. The majority of the game doesn't have much of a story you complete random quest and get stronger and some of your starting heroes have character specific quests but not all of them. I would prefer it if the game had no story (Mount and blade doesn't have one) but the last quest of the game dumps the story on the player giving long unskippable flashback sequences and hitting the player with lore at the very end of the game. The story goes like this; you bring peace to Salzaar and then you are betrayed and war starts up again, you confront the betrayer and beat them but the game tells you that you lost and teleports you to the other side of the game world and you have to go back and fight them again. You beat them again but the game tells you that you lost again and teleports you through time where you get a lore dump. In the past you are betrayed once again by someone that you have been told the whole game is the savior of humanity then are dropped into the present where you are betrayed by one of your companions before fighting the final boss. An easy recommend for the bargain bin price: 8/10. Plenty of content even in early access, surpassing many triple AAAAYYYY games out there. Very high replayability with a wide array of skillsets to choose from during character creation to tweak your own unique build. That being said, there're a couple of things I've got issues with:

1) The combat is janky & unwieldy. Biggest problem is the pace, you have time to issue ONE order (attack/defend/follow) to whatever army group (melee/ranged/cav) you have before the enemy is on you (usually under 3sec, less if they have cav) & everything devolves into a messy brawl: melee & cav bump & slide around each other while ranged troops run around like headless chickens. You simply don't have the time to use proper troop tactics in combat, you're much better off using those precious few seconds to fire off your hero skills before you get swarmed again. Simply allowing the player to pause or slow down combat to issue orders will make things SOOOO much better.

2) But the single most annoying thing about this game: ITEM DURABILITY. Everything other than your mount & trade goods break, even your trinkets. They break even if you don't take any damage, simply engaging in combat will suffice. Worse still, you can't just head to the nearest town & click repair items to handle it for a price. Oh no, you're got to buy tools from a small handful of towns that sell them and then repair your items individually. An unnecessary & frustrating waste of time. I really hope that an option to disable this 'mechanic' is included before full release and if not, I wish only bad things on the person(s) who decided to implement this crap into an otherwise outstanding NON-SURVIVAL game.

There are some potentially interesting RPG mechanics here, but that's about the limit of the good I can see in it as of yet. I've played less than an hour and been in half a dozen fights, yet the combat already feels like a dull, repetitive chore. It somehow feels like playing a decade old browser game trying to imitate Diablo with a tiny splash of Mount & Blade, but I can't even fully explain how it manages to pull off that feeling.

Currently on the fence if I want to refund the game, or gamble on it getting better (or at least less of a chore) after you build up a bigger group and engage in bigger fights.

An underwhelming experience: all the necessary parts are there, but everything is clunky or undercooked. "Sands of Salzaar" didn't strike me as a bad game during an hour I spent with it, but I got a strong feeling that it needs a few more years of development time.

Fun game, a little grindy but the progression is very satisfying early on. Sadly it suffers from the same issue as bannerlord (imo) where it becomes less fun the more cities you have to manage. I think the progression becomes less and less satisfying the deeper you get in the game. It's a very deep game, but the end game doesnt feel very complete. It also suffers balancing issues like bannerlord, like how you can just spam craft spears and sell them to every city for excessive money then proceed to win the game with your unlimited gold in banner, in salzaar you can just spam buy thur rams and watch them bulldoze everything without even costing jade (a rare currency commonly used to upgrade rare or high tier units).

I'll give an example, let's say you find a weapon you really like, because of a unique effect that you can make entire really neat build around. Guess what? If that effect is unique to the weapon you wont ever see it again in a higher level version. Maybe it's like that for balancing reasons but it doesnt feel like there are too many choices for gear. You just run the highest lvl dungeons and make your character around whatever is available, which means you're limited to one to two unique effects per weapon type (aside from the random stats/effects you get).  

Here's an example of one the things that start to feel not so satisfying. In the beginning after you realize you want to recruit the strong heroes as soon as possible, its fun going town to town seeing who's there and running errands for the first few heroes you like cause its super satisfying once you have them in your party. Missed one or two heroes you really wanted? Thats okay after you've done enough dungeons youll probably have more then enough gifts to have at least one or two that they will like, then combined with an errand or two you can poach them from their faction. Now here's where it gets lame, once you start your own force you need to start recruiting as many heroes as you can cause youll need to leave them in towns to manage and defend them, or do things for your force. This means they wont even be in your party, which is fine, but you'll also have to go around gifting and running errands for whoever you can. In fact it's recommended that you get your favor/reputation up with as many heroes as you can before you even start your own force since it makes you declare war on everyone. 

Endgame seems to be just doing NG+ on a higher difficulty, and I love the NG+ concept, especially with the legacy points system since it encourages you to just do whatever on your first run to figure stuff out while you grind legacy points for your next run. End game on your new save will probably just be picking a class(es) and arcana you like, then grinding wisdom crystals. This would be more fun if there was content that required you being that strong. 

I actually enjoyed the stories and side quests. Im not a story type of guy, I always skip rpg dialogue and story, but even the side stories were really interesting and fun, lots of plot twists and surprises. It reminded me of the old final fantasy games, final fantasy 1 specifically, where you find quests randomly just from exploring around and there's no hand holding to progress it, but youll probably progress your quests on your own anyways just playing the game. It's a more natural flow that I enjoy, rather than a linear experience where youre just trying to brute force your way to the next part in a railroad of events. 

That said there are a lot of things that will frustrate you to no end.. like trying to find people, and some quests will completely stump you. 

Honestly most of the game issues can be fixed with mods. Like the issue of jade farming being really hard, theres a mod for that makes it just slightly easier without making you feel like youre cheaing, etc. Overall this game is a very solid 8.5/10. I was not expecting much tbh, it was way better than I thought. Easily worth the full price. I hope it keeps improving. Game is still getting frequent updates which is really cool to see too.

Salzaar is not the best action combat in gaming. It's not the best sandbox game. It's not that great as an RPG. The translation is pretty rough in a lot of places, though nothing that I've never been able to figure out.

But the sum of it's parts add up to still be something I still really enjoy. You go from an individual bum wandering around aimlessly to leading an army of troops taking over a nation and commanding other armies as well; while your own character has gone from getting beat up by some random bandits to cleaving through the front line of an army. It's a very satisfying feeling regardless of the rough spots on the way there. I also feel the classes play pretty varied for multiple runs and hero compositions can change things up between runs as well.

Ultimately whether the rough spots are a deal breaker or not is going to vary for everyone, but at even the full $15 price tag I think it's worth a bit of a risk for anyone who likes the premise of it. There's not really a huge set of games that give that individual to army / zero to hero combination, and all of them have their own shares of rough spots I've been more than willing to endure.

Also I recommend anyone who plays to immediately turn on quick casting for everything - as it makes the combat feel much better than click confirms.

I'm genuinely curious to see these developers do more content, because if they had a little more money they could probably make something interesting, but this just isn't it yet

[i][b]As someone who played this game in the last weeks I'm going to answer some questions you might are interested, if you don't own the game yet and want to know if it's good or bad.[/b][/i]

[h3]What is this game about?[/h3]
I would describe this game as a mix of: 
[i]M&B + Diablo/PoE + own unique asian artstyle[/i]
If you know games like [i]Battle Brothers[/i] or [i]Kenshi[/i], they might can be compared as well.

[u]Why M&B?[/u]
- walk through the land with your Squad,
- kill bandit groups or raid caravans,
- do quests, 
- recruit different kind of troops & upgrade them, 
- trade to get rich,
- siege to conquer a town (or everything),
- war/ally with factions,
- build your own faction or join one,
- start a romance with a female character,
- recruit heroes

[u]Why PoE/Diablo?[/u]
- grind dungeons/caves for legendary items (& monsters like dragon/demon/phoenix, if enabled),
- level system & skill system,
- skill tree for talents (via prestige),
- challenge bosses to get better gear
- choose your character from different classes (or play as nameless to combine two or more classes)! Use magic, be an assassin or be a magic using assassin, your choice!


[h3]Is the game fun in the long run and does it have a high level of replayability?[/h3]
I would say [i][b]yes[/b][/i].
There are three reasons for it.
The first and most important one is the [b]legacy system[/b].
You can do specific challenges, clear caves, conquer towns and get their treasures to get legacy points. These legacy points can be used to get benefits on your next run. If you have enough legacy points you can unluck the nameless class, where you are able to combine two or more classes like mentioned above. Playing a different class makes this game more replayable because it won't be the same like the last run since you will have a different playstyle and different skills. Combining them makes it even more replayable.
The second one is the [b]increased unlimited difficulty[/b]. 
Once you finish the main quest and win the final fight you can increase the difficulty of your next run by +1. There is no limit. This also gives you legacy points.
The third one is the [b]enableable expert mode[/b], where you only have one savegame. 
At first this one gives you legacy points as well. It also makes this game harder in a way, that everything that happens is irreversible. It prevents you from save scum, which I really recommend. You might not win all battles. Losing is part of the game, but you will get stronger and stronger.


[h3]Would I recommend this game in it's current state?[/h3]
[i][b]Yes[/b][/i]!
If you like the games listed above you will definitely have fun here.
The start can be a bit hard but once you are into it, you will be on a roll.
The price is really cheap for what it is offering already. 
But keep in mind that it's early access, you will encounter one or the other bug.
The game has a high risk of addiction. I played it too long in a row and got red eyes because of that!

They made some effort to at least put level suggestions on bandit camps and such, but everything else is just an easy win or a completely unwinnable fight. The absolute hands down WORST part of combat is all the stunlocks you (the player) get stuck in from getting chain knocked, stunned, frozen, etc. This *maybe* acceptable for army units, but for the player character there absolutely NEEDS to be some kind of small immunity window after getting crowd controlled. It feels really really bad for instance- to have 5-10 camel riders decide to ignore your army and focus on you for 2 minutes and you can't even move or cast spells the entire time until you die.

Combat balance is made especially obvious when you are attacking a city- the defending team has an overwhelming advantage in that they receive something like 20 completely free reinforcements about every 30 seconds (possibly due to barracks buildings?.) Even with a reasonably maxed out army of ~20 squads all level 20 and spells that can wipe out 15 enemies at a time you cannot win fast enough to overcome the constant free reinforcements.
