Sands of Salzaar is an ambitious open-world action RPG that blends elements of strategy, sandbox exploration, and light storytelling in a stylized fantasy desert setting. Set in a world left fractured after the fall of a great empire, the game drops you into the shoes of a wandering hero navigating political unrest, territorial conflict, and arcane mysteries. The tone is one of slow-burning discovery—players aren’t guided by rigid objectives but encouraged to chart their own course, making decisions that shape the landscape in subtle and sometimes dramatic ways. Right from the start, you’re given access to a large and interconnected map, with various regions controlled by different factions, each pursuing their own goals. It’s a world that reacts to your choices and movements, where a simple skirmish between bandits can ripple into a city changing hands if you're not paying attention. This dynamism is one of the game’s strongest suits, even when some systems feel undercooked or unrefined.

Character creation is surprisingly robust, offering a variety of starting classes—from spell-slinging Ifrits to beastmasters, duelists, and elemental monks—each with their own unique skills and story hooks. Alternatively, you can start with a custom class, tailoring your ability tree for a personalized experience. The game doesn't rush you toward any goal, so whether you want to amass wealth through trading, lead armies into conquest, or focus on completing regional quests, it all depends on your playstyle. That freedom is where Sands of Salzaar shines brightest. The core loop involves exploring the world, building your army, completing quests for gold and items, and ultimately either supporting or undermining the dominant factions. You can even establish your own power base by capturing cities and defending them from rival claimants. While this creates a compelling rise-from-nothing arc, it’s also easy to get lost without a clear direction, especially early on. The game expects you to figure out its logic through trial and error, which can be frustrating for players used to more guided experiences.

Combat is where the game falters for many. On the surface, it presents a real-time strategy-light system where you command troops and heroes across sprawling battlefields. In practice, however, fights often devolve into chaotic, unreadable brawls. Unit AI can be unreliable, and the lack of precise control makes larger battles feel more like number contests than tactical engagements. Your hero can use flashy abilities and dodge-roll mechanics to carve through enemies, but the responsiveness and feedback are inconsistent. While some players adapt and grow to enjoy the messiness, others find it tiresome. For all the effort put into troop progression—leveling units, promoting them into elite variants, and equipping your heroes—there's little tactical nuance. The spectacle of a large battle is impressive in scale, but it rarely demands much strategic thought beyond overwhelming force.

The RPG elements are expansive, even if occasionally overwhelming. You’re constantly leveling up not only your main character but your recruited heroes, managing armies, trading goods between cities, and exploring dungeons for rare loot. Skill trees are deep and offer diverse builds, which encourages experimentation across multiple playthroughs. A legacy system lets you carry progress forward between runs, gradually unlocking better starting perks and gear. This long-term structure is ideal for players who enjoy investing in incremental growth and seeing their power snowball over time. However, the interface for managing these systems is clunky at times, and the game doesn’t always explain key mechanics well. There are moments when you’ll stare at menus or troop screens unsure of what a specific stat does or whether your choices are meaningful.

Graphically, Sands of Salzaar operates on a budget, but its charm is undeniable. The character portraits are hand-drawn in a bold, expressive art style, and the overworld features painterly desert vistas, shifting sandstorms, and vibrant city hubs that evoke a strong atmosphere. Though the battlefield visuals are more functional than impressive, the game compensates with a stylized UI and some imaginative spell effects. The music is subtle but effective, evoking the exotic fantasy tone with Middle Eastern and Asian influences. However, one of the game’s persistent issues is its English localization, which remains rough even post-launch. Dialogues often read awkwardly, and many quest texts suffer from grammatical errors or unclear instructions. While the core narrative isn’t the centerpiece of the game, these translation problems break immersion and can make key story moments feel flat.

Technically, the game is relatively stable on PC, though not without its quirks. Players have reported occasional crashes, inconsistent resolution scaling, and UI glitches, especially when changing settings mid-session. The mobile ports are less reliable, with reports of language settings reverting to Chinese and story modes becoming unstable after extended play. That said, the developers have demonstrated a commitment to updates, releasing balance patches and new content post-launch. Modding support is also present, which has allowed some players to tweak mechanics or fix annoyances. It’s clear that the developers had a strong vision—they simply lacked the resources to fully polish the experience.

Despite its flaws, Sands of Salzaar is a compelling game for players who enjoy forging their own story in a reactive world. Its sandbox design, freedom of choice, and large-scale battles echo the spirit of games like Mount & Blade or Battle Brothers, while the RPG systems give it a progression depth that keeps you invested for dozens of hours. It’s not a game for everyone—those looking for tight combat mechanics, a strong central story, or polished presentation may find themselves frustrated. But for the patient and curious, it offers a vast playground where your choices matter and every run can unfold differently. It’s an impressive feat for an indie project, one that manages to be greater than the sum of its sometimes clunky parts.

A mixed experience, but entertaining. The game is very flawed but has an entertaining gameplay loop and a lot of potential if some of the flaws are fixed. I'll start off with the bad parts so that I can end with the good. 
1) Bad translation. This isn't unusual for a chinese game. But some parts in dialogue are particularly egregious and in general sap all immersion. A lot of scenarios reminiscent of those youtube ads for mobile games that don't exist. A few menus have small portions still in chinese, but most are translated fine. Mainly just the dialogue that is wonky. 
2) Memory leak. The game gets slower and slower to save and traverse through map areas the longer you have it running. If you play the game for more than like 8 hours in a sitting it will take like a minute to traverse areas. Clearly a memory leak, needs fixing. 
3) Lame story/sidequests. This is partially due to the translation, but in general all the side quests and story quests are very uncompelling. At their best they are just very anime and uninteresting, at their worst they are mistranslated nonsense. But it's a mount and blade type game so you don't play it for story. 
4) Combat. A shame really. It tries to go for an Arpg + M&B type thing. You control your character from a top down view whilst your army does its thing. Uses league of legends type controls. Tactics are basically non existent. There is a menu for it but honestly, its a waste of time, the battles are too quick. You can't issue commands as the armies close in like you can in mount and blade or starsector. Combat is also really clunky. Especially tavern fights are REALLY clunky. Overall just not very fun unless you have particular builds (knight errant is fun). 

Mixed points: 
1) World design. The world in general is uninteresting and uninspired. It has some locations I like a lot, like the Umbra cliffs and Twinluna valley. But if you asked me to tell you the difference between West docana desert, crying rock, and redstone valley, I wouldn't have an answer. 
2) Factions. I can see what they were going for. Nasir have a balanced military with a bit of everything, makes sense as they were the biggest remnant of the old empire. Dakn have mainly ranged units, all units are light armor, they prefer to use poison and such. Dhib don't have much unique about them besides their cool animal hats. Thur are heavily armored units, with the tankiest units in the game, as well as unique siege weapons. Akhal are the cavalry based faction. The issue is that The factions don't have very good unit cohesion within their own faction, you kinda gotta mix and match in order to have a good army. This is a problem for doing faction based runs that a lot of people (including me) like to do in mount and blade type games. Thur units are so slow that their ranged units tend to run in front of their melee troops, because the melee troops walk at a snails pace. Dakn troops are super squishy and just get ran down, in fact, dakn has such bad unit cohesion that they get eliminated by the AI pretty early in every run. They have cool scorpions though. Nasir is the only faction with a balanced military, so they basically always take over large swathes of the map. The AI doesn't react to snowballing factions well either. So basically only you, the player, can stop them. 
3) Music. There are some good tracks. They are just too short and play constantly, unlike games like kenshi that give the music time to breathe but have bangers every once and a while. 

Good things:
1) Customization. This is the main good thing about the game. It has very very very good customization. There are some premade classes availible, but you can pick skills using legacy points that you earn in your runs to slap additional skills onto effectively a second skill tree, to spec skill points into as well. Once you beat the game you unlock a unique class where you essentially just build your own skill tree, making an eldrich horror out of all the skill trees of the other classes, or making your own fresh one. There are gems that you earn throughout the run that you can slot into units that give them bonuses and stuff, and you can customize your units further with this. Party member skill trees are also customizable so you can have your party member play off your strengths or make up for your weaknesses, etc. 
2) Unit variety. Even though the factions units don't dont work that well together if only using one factions units, there is still a lot of variety and some cool ones. Especially the secret units, though how you get them is a little wonky. From infantry that summon crows, to ballista, to giant demons, to dragons, to snake people, there are a lot of unique units, with their own upgrade trees. 

Conclusion: 
Overall, if you like mount and blade type games, played all the others and want more, then consider it. Especially if it is on sale, don't quite think its worth full price at the moment. I got it for 6 bucks. It's extremely janky and you might walk away dissapointed, but I found it entertaining at least. It has a ton of flaws but overall has a lot of potential and I hope it gets some issues fixed and becomes a great game in the future.

Sands of Salzaar is fine. I wish I could say better things about it, but it's a budget Mount & Blade at its core. 

The ARPG system looks and feels pretty good, but it's not very deep at all. The level cap feels very low and it seems like you can max a character out extremely easily and early. ARPGs have always felt a little weaker to me as soon as your character is max level. The mechanics are also rather opaque due to a lack of roll-over text.

The overworld is both over and underwhelming. It's overwhelming due to the number of events you hear about, most of which are pointless. Apparently all the adventurers in the world are constantly having minor events and you hear about ALL of them ALL the time. I quickly learned to tune out all the event messages because most of them are irrelevant. Unfortunately, that leads to the underwhelming portion, as when I hear about ALL of the events NONE of them are important. I'm pretty sure there were major exchanges of territory and battles occurring while I was running around doing quests and leveling up, but I didn't learn about any of it. The world felt pretty dead to me, despite the fact that it really wasn't. The game needs event filters or different default event filters. I don't care if a random NPC had a heartwarming conversation with widow. I DO care if the Nasir are taking over the continent.

Finally, the translation is lacking. The story would be a lot more engaging if I could get more from the writing than the gist of it. It would also go a long way towards helping me understand some of the mechanics.

Overall, I still have to recommend the game because it's priced like a budget Mount & Blade. If you can't afford Bannerlord or your computer can't run it, this is a good alternative. It's also still being patched so it should be interesting to see where the game goes over time. Maybe they can fix some of the issues.

Just finished story as Sentinel (focused on swapping auras to buff allies with small bursts of personal damage), haven't tried Sandbox yet. I liked it overall. It plays like Diablo in a Mount & Blade setting, but isn't individually as expansive in gameplay style as either of the two. 

Your own character can become relatively OP towards the endgame, but not to the point where it can solo an entire army and make the strategic layer irrelevant, as enemy leaders also level up similarly.

Pros:
+ Gameplay is generally fun if you like building up your character while seeing huge unit blobs fighting it out and spending time convincing powerful characters to join your side
+ The aesthetic is cozy, reminds me of classic CRPGs
+ Trying to minmax your unit composition is fun
+ Devs seem to be actively improving the game
+ Mod support is always a good thing; nothing too groundbreaking seems to be out yet, but the game was only recently fully released
+ Losing a battle usually doesn't fully wipe your squad, which is a great thing given how expensive it is to reach high level compositions

Cons:
- I only found out time acceleration exists as a random tip several hours in, that should really show up sooner (Hold ctrl for anyone who also didn't know)
- Inventory management is a pain
- Limited quest selection between town and character favors, they get repetitive pretty fast
- Battle/map load times get progressively slower while playing until a game restart, there's probably a memory leak somewhere
- No way to test out how certain squads would work, you commit to units before you know what they do
- Map AI needs more work, can't fight grouped battles outside of sieges
- Settlement development doesn't really feel meaningful
- When you run your own tribe, managing your companions/leaders is kind of poorly optimized from a UX perspective, hard to keep track of who's where and doing what, and they also don't seem to ever go on the offensive on their own. This last point might be since I wasn't playing on max difficulty, though.
- Endgame is mainly running to the same jade chests from bandit camps and repeating two dragon fights on a fixed timer to get jade and skill points for the extra oomph on the character level, strategically you try to win one town at a time

So in short, the pros are that it's a fun idea, executed decently enough, with a suitable aesthetic, and the cons are that the game still has a lot of jank especially surrounding the strategic layer and endgame content. It's not for everyone, but if you can't get enough of personally leading armies in games, it's worth a try. I'm hoping the devs spend more time polishing the game, I think it has a solid core in place.

One extremely addictive game (I completed campaign three times in a row). Campaign is not that much relevant (same outcome), but everything else... WOW!
Like Mount&Blade set in Chinese culture and mythology.
Your hero can learn different combat, magic and passive skills with various effects (even learn skills from other followers and traders).
Recruit various types of warriors (and creatures), evolve them in different ways (both in fighting style and tiers of strength) and equip various gems for bonus skills.
Recruit several heroes (out of at least hundred) for your group (some even have their own mini-quests), upgrade them and give them various equipment. Later give your heroes chance to guard your cities (or even reward them to rule some of them on their own) or even have their own armies and they fight others in your name.
You have love-hate relationship with several clans and you can decide who will be your ally or enemy (or make them all your allies or enemies). You will even have opportunity to start your own clan...or even some random rogue hero might conquer a city and start your own clan.
Your cities can be upgraded to give your more money and resources every week.
Battlefields are hectic, chaotic and hilarious, especially when you use high level skills that can change the tide of the battle.
Do quests, trade items, wander the several different regions and hunt monsters and outlaws...or do all of it.
Start new game with some new bonuses and challenges.

The choice is yours.

P.S - I also have Android version of the game (that looks identical)...though I am afraid to use it on my mobile because that is how much is this game addictive.

Two thumbs up and absolute recommendation! 😁

Similar to Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord, but with an emphasis on questing and gear grinding. There are a few translation issues here and there, but overall the game is great! I feel like the reason that the game isn't doing as good as it could be is because there doesn't seem to be any dedicated wiki.

Cartoon Bannorlord type game. Honestly had a LOT of potential to be a great game but it seems like the developers have abandoned it. English translation is super spotty, okay in some places, really bad in others. Lots of small bugs and jankiness that NEED to be addressed. There is alot to do and impressive unit variety but theres just too much holding the game back for me to sink time into. If this game were to be revived by the developers I would definitely recommend playing.

Diablo meet Mount and Blade and have a hentai night. Result could be this game...

All sounds like a promising breed, but not for me. It is too much of all and so it is nothing. Also too much text for action focus.
Missing the "beeing in a battle" of M&B, also missing the overkill fun of Diablo.

Maybe I made something wrong for not get the hype, yet I will deinstall and maybe retry in a year.
Advertised as coop a while back anymore, I'd honestly like a refund at this point, only bought it to play with friends.

It's a pretty fun game, It's an auto battler but gives the player agency as an in game unit that is controllable by the player. It reminds me of DOTA in some ways. But the world map is pretty massive too so there's a lot of exploration that can be done. There's a mod community out there too and quite a few mods for the game. Although, the game isn't fully translated to English yet it's still quite playable and enjoyable, and the translation that has been done so far is easy to read and understand. The art direction for the characters looks good and there is player character customization. There's a meta progression in the game in the form of "legacy" points which will allow subsequent new characters created by the player to be stronger so long as the previous character got farther than the character before it. Hopefully the way I said that makes sense. I got the game on sale, but it's really not that expensive in the first place. I'd say it's a very good game for the price.

I wanted to give this a positive review, but it hasn't been updated in over a year. The english translations used feel awkward at best and the phrasing leaves you pondering what they really meant. The combat is okay-ish. Sometimes the pathing of troops breaks and you need to literally push troops forwards. Some move descriptions are deceptive, saying it effects enemies but it also harms your own troops. (Again, this is likely a translation issue.) 

The character customization is great. You can make them look how you want, you pick several characters and build them up more or less how you want. This truly is where this game shines. There is town/city/faction building that I have not reached yet, but has potential.

Addictive time-waster, yes it is like bannerlord, it also reminds me a bit of an old flash game called feudalism, you can just get lost mindlessly in here for hours and not realize how time has passed, very fun.
